🇺🇸 US retailers: Target - Switch 2 console: check stock Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Best Buy - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- 🇬🇧 UK retailers: Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Smyths Toys - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- Latest LIVE updates
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has launched, and it's glorious. But the real challenge isn't saving Hyrule as Link; it's finding a restock of the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Nintendo Switch 2 console.
Restocks are rolling out — Target and Nintendo recently dropped fresh chances to grab the hard-to-find console — and with Nintendo promising more stock is on the way, I'm bringing you the latest stock updates.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . However, multiple retailers are prioritizing in-store restocks (Best Buy, Walmart, GameStop), so if you can, be sure to check your nearest locations.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years, and know how to secure in-demand items. Below are all the links you need, alongside live updates on Zelda Switch 2 restocks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
I've been checking all the retailers every so often, but I've just done a full retailer sweep to see what's available.
A whole lot of nearly nothing.
The one place I was able to see was on Target. There's a button that will show you stores with stock near you. For me, it was one store with one console in stock about 10 miles away.
If you have gas in the car and a minute, this might be the way to get your special Switch 2.
If you didn't know there are two versions of the cover art for the Ocarina of Time remake. One with foil texture and one without.
Apparently, the retails have all swapped out the foil cover on their listings for the standard edition.
You may get lucky if you try your luck in-store, but online it appears out of stock.
GameStop is showing the Zelda console as out of stock but the Pro Controller might still be available. However, the retailer has been pushing in-store so you won't be able to get it on the website.
I called my local GameStop and they were out of stock, but you might have better luck with your closest store.
I just did a sweep through the retailers, and it looks like the only thing available is the 40th anniversary Pro Controller for $213.99 at Walmart , which is double the normal $99 price, but cheaper than what I'm seeing on Best Buy (showing as sold out).
Nothing to report at present, Target has now returned to "sold out", though perhaps we'll see a third restock later today, meanwhile no signs of any stock at Walmart so the rumors are unfortunately looking increasingly unlikely. In-store remains your chance to find a Zelda Switch 2 , so if you live locally to a retailer, it's worth trying your luck. Meanwhile, my day is winding down, but I'll be handing over to a colleague shortly, to make sure you don't miss any restocks.
Quick update on the Target situation, I'm no longer seeing the "add to cart" button, but it does direct me to "show in-store stock" with at least one location popping up claiming to have stock nearby. It would seem all the online inventory has been snapped up, but I would still recommend checking for now, you could get lucky. And Target has restocked online twice now, could it go for a third?
I didn't see this one coming, but the "add to cart" button has just returned on Target, so get over there and see if you can secure a Zelda Switch 2 as it looks like stock is returning at the retailer!
All eyes are on Walmart at present, there are rumors flying around they will restock the Zelda Switch 2 today, but so far nothing. Remember, as I keep saying, there's no confirmation here, but restock rumors often prove to have some truth to them, so fingers firmly crossed the noise around Walmart amounts to a drop.
Well, after about an hour, I'm not seeing any signs of available stock at Target, even with a lot of refreshes, so I feel pretty confident saying the retailer is once again sold out . Hopefully you were able to grab one in this latest Zelda Switch 2 restock. If not, don't worry, I'm still here tracking stock levels across retailers. Remember, Walmart is rumored to drop next.
Target was the big one today, and after restocking in the very early morning hours, I wondered if that would be the retailer sold out again, but a second restock has appeared online. The console is going to sell out fast, so get over there, and even if you get a "sold out" message at first, keep trying, as more stock could appear.
No time for talking, the Zelda Switch 2 is IN STOCK at Target, go grab yours!!!
Last night after a busy day of restock tracking, I finally got to sink my teeth into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and while I'm very early in my quest, my first impressions are that it's a glorious remake.
Our reviewer, Anthony Spadafora, had a similar experience, calling it "even better than my childhood memories." You can read his full Ocarina of Time review if you're looking to fill some time until we have more restock news to bring you.
Rumors have been flying around this week that Walmart could restock the Zelda Switch 2 from November 6 (aka today). This is based on an unverified leak of an internal document suggesting that the national retailer was gearing up for a restock. Again, this is all unconfirmed, but it's the retailer to watch right now, and it has already this week restocked in-store, so could an online drop follow today?
One of the big themes this week has been retailers opting for in-store restocks rather than dropping stock online.
I've just checked some local Target stores, and the retailer's online tracker is telling me there is Zelda Switch 2's available at nearby locations. However it's very limited ("only 1 left"), and these in-store stock trackers aren't always updated in realtime, so even if it tells you there's stock there's no guarantees.
Still, if you've got your heart set on securing a Zelda Switch 2, and have a Target store within reasonable distance (I wouldn't recommend a lengthy roadtrip), then getting down to your nearest location might be your best chance of getting one.
It looks like Target opted for a late-night online restock based on what I've seen on social media, so if you're still on the hunt for a Zelda Switch 2, that's the place to check now. But I'm seeing conflicting reports, with some users claiming that no stock was available, so I'll keep watching the retailer for signs of more stock.
Good morning! Rory here, it's a new day, and I'm back online to track Zelda Switch 2 restock across retailers. Today (Nov. 6) is set to be a big day with at least one online restock confirmed at Target, and there could be more on the way, too.
Once more,

articles.title_orig: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest after bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Ousted Paraguayan president placed under house arrest after bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
The leader had offered to resign, but lawmakers went ahead with proceedings to strip him of immunity granted to former presidents
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena was placed under house arrest on Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.
Pena had offered his resignation over the disaster, but lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings that would strip him of immunity granted to former presidents.
He did not attend the trial in the Senate despite earlier pledging to defend himself.

articles.title_orig: Reflections | After US midterms, how bitter political divisions eroded 4 Chinese dynasties
articles.title_zh: Reflections | After US midterms, how bitter political divisions eroded 4 Chinese dynasties
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump and the Republicans struggle to spin a historic defeat in the US midterms.
It was the most expensive election in American history: nearly $12bn spent, much of it on advertisements, with the majority of that money going to Republican candidates. But most voters weren’t buying it. The result: a Democratic sweep on a scale not seen in half a century.
In the aftermath of the vote, United States President Donald Trump – who has long revelled in his ability to turn controversy and crisis into spectacle – appeared to lose control of the narrative. The scale of the Republican defeat amounts to a repudiation of Trump’s politics and the US-Israel war on Iran. Meenakshi Ravi and Richard Gizbert examine the political and media fallout.
Contributors: Alex Shephard – Senior editor, The New Republic Rob Arlett – former Trump state campaign chair & Republican strategist Maya Berry – Executive director, Arab American Institute
Serbia’s new political leadership has yet to form a government, but the country’s media institutions are already being purged of voices who gave former president, Aleksandar Vucic, years of favourable coverage. Tariq Nafi looks at the news outlets being held to account.
Equator magazine is the brainchild of a group of writers and editors – some of them ex-mainstream media – who came together during a “moment of moral despair” as they witnessed Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza unfold. One year after its launch, Equator has produced some quality stories and essays on global politics, culture and art – all presented with an eye for design. We speak to cofounder and former Guardian editor, Jonathan Shainin, about the magazine’s vision and how it’s going.
Featuring: Jonathan Shainin – Founding Editor, Equator magazine

The U.S. is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation assistance for information about Iran's nuclear program, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Friday.
In a post on X, CENTCOM highlighted the State Department's Rewards for Justice program, which is seeking information about Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel involved in the program.
The reward also covers information about the movement of nuclear-related materials, equipment or personnel, including individuals in the scientific community.
The announcement comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran while Washington and Tehran continue negotiations over the country's nuclear program.
Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military operations targeting Tehran's nuclear facilities.
Iran is demanding concrete action from Washington before advancing nuclear negotiations, with a senior official saying Friday that Tehran will no longer rely on written U.S. commitments.
Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, accused Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments over the past 18 months, according to state-run IRNA, as reported by Iran International.
“Iran needs to see the US’s practical actions, and [then] the groundwork for opening a new chapter would be prepared,” Bagheri said.
The remarks come as Washington reviews a nuclear proposal submitted by Tehran through Qatari intermediaries, while President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran.
President Donald Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military strikes against Tehran's nuclear facilities.
Speaking at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, Trump credited American B-2 bombers with preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
"And you know what? If they did have it, if we didn't go in with those beautiful B-2 bombers a little more than a year ago, if I allowed them to have it today, there would be no Israel. It would have been wiped off the face of the earth, and there would be no Middle East," Trump said.
"We will never let that happen. Iran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. You can rest assured," the president added.
Trump's remarks come as his administration considers renewed military operations against Iran while continuing diplomatic negotiations with Tehran over its nuclear program.
Qatar pushed back Friday against reports suggesting negotiations between the United States and Iran had collapsed, insisting that both countries are continuing efforts to reach an agreement.
In a statement, Qatar's International Media Office rejected online reports alleging that Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani had said Washington and Tehran failed to reach a deal.
The office accused unnamed parties of misrepresenting the prime minister's comments and spreading misinformation to undermine diplomatic efforts.
"His Excellency’s remarks have been deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability in our region," the statement read. "Many of these claims are being spread by fake accounts trying to undermine diplomatic efforts and push for further escalation. This is deeply irresponsible. His Excellency stated today that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal."
Qatar said its mediators remain in close contact with both countries as negotiations continue.
Three incoming Jewish members of Congress are calling for the release of Arab journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, who was detained in Israel after interviewing a fugitive former lawmaker.
Brad Lander, Steve Weiner and Daniel Biss sent a letter to Israeli Ambassador to the U.S. Yechiel Leiter expressing concern about Abu Shehadeh's detention, according to The Times of Israel.
The journalist was arrested Tuesday after interviewing former Israeli lawmaker Azmi Bishara, who fled Israel in 2007 amid suspicions that he aided Hezbollah during the previous year's war in Lebanon.
The lawmakers said Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of contact with a foreign agent and that the allegations against him remain sealed.
They called for his release, arguing that interviewing controversial political figures is a fundamental part of journalism.
Lufthansa Group is reportedly changing flight operations to Israel to prevent crew members from staying overnight in the country through Nov. 30 as concerns grow over renewed fighting with Iran .
The airline group, which operates Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines and ITA Airways, plans to use crew-change stops in Athens and Larnaca, Cyprus, for certain flights, according to Israel's N12 News, as cited by The Jerusalem Post.
The adjustments could result in schedule changes or cancellations for some passengers.
The reported restrictions come as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran following meetings with his national security team this week.
Washington and Tehran are also continuing diplomatic negotiations over Iran's nuclear program.
The Trump administration announced sanctions Friday against eight Canada-based currency exchange businesses accused of helping Iran evade U.S. financial restrictions.
The Treasury Department said the businesses facilitated transactions involving sanctioned Iranian entities, including cryptocurrency activity linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
Several businesses also allegedly helped launder drug proceeds tied to former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, according to Treasury.
The sanctions come as Washington and Tehran continue nuclear negotiations, with Iran demanding relief from U.S. economic restrictions as part of a proposed agreement.
A student-run food festival at Northwestern University was canceled after several campus organizations objected to the inclusion of a pro- Israel student group, according to reports.
The event, organized by Spoon University Northwestern, faced opposition after Wildcats for Israel was invited to participate. Three student organizations issued a joint statement criticizing the group's involvement, while nearly all participating groups reportedly withdrew from the festival.
Organizers subsequently removed Wildcats for Israel from the event and apologized for its inclusion, according to The Times of Israel.
The Daily Northwestern reported that the festival was ultimately canceled following the dispute.
California Post opinion editor Joel Pollak defended President Donald Trump's handling of the Iran war Friday, arguing that Americans will eventually appreciate his decisions despite the political fallout from the midterm elections.
Speaking on Fox News' "Life, Liberty & Levin," Pollak said Trump had fulfilled his campaign promises by confronting Iran and securing the U.S. border, even when those decisions carried political consequences.
"Trump had a responsibility that he took seriously to do what was in the national interest," Pollak said. "Sometimes being president means you have to make those tough decisions."
Pollak argued that previous administrations had avoided confronting Tehran because of the potential political repercussions.
"This is why nobody confronted Iran, because it has a political cost. But in the long run, the American people will be grateful for it," he said.
Pollak also compared Trump's political challenges to those faced by former President Ronald Reagan, noting that Reagan lost eight Senate seats during his sixth year in office but later became widely respected.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: North Korea's army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
articles.title_zh: North Korea's army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
articles.content_orig:
Billions of dollars of crypto stolen — in a hack that we’re now learning involved corporate vibe coding efforts. You couldn’t come up with a more quintessential cautionary tale for an era when employers are embracing AI at every level.
After hackers drained nearly $6.3 billion from the crypto platform , Binance has revealed how the thieves pulled off what might be the heist of the century.
In a detailed report on its investigation published Tuesday, the company described an elaborate scheme that took place over months involving sham job interviews, old-fashioned phishing, and — yes — a hijacked AI tool.
It began in June when an employee on Binance’s wallet developer team thought they’d indulge in some vibe coding by installing a popular AI coding tool. But they ended up downloading a tampered installation of Homebrew, a tool that’s popular with software engineers, after clicking a malicious ad. Binance said it detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and changed relevant credentials.
So far so good, except that the attack exposed the role of the employee and his colleagues on the wallet team to the hackers, giving them the opening they needed. From there, some classic social engineering went into play. A hacker, posing as a project director, reached out to another software engineer through a legitimate job-hunting platform to offer an interview first with an “HR representative” and then the “CEO” of a fake company.
The fraudsters then earned the employee’s trust by sharing a social media account with personal photos and videos, something that Binance said “was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” (It’s unclear from the report, but perhaps these were fabricated with AI, adding another element of AI menace to this story.)
Crucially, the follow-up interview was conducted over text. The engineer was asked to complete and download an “assignment” that contained malicious code that instantly executed once the employee began installing it. Among the things it changed was replacing a real development tool with a malicious version that could communicate with the hackers and execute commands.
That all took place in September. Starting in October, the hacker used the compromised employee machine to leverage an internal AI tool and use it as a “springboard” to seize control of the computer and the computer of a third wallet developer. From there, they used credentials stolen from the first wallet team employee to log into the third employee’s computer and trigger a malicious script that launched the attack.
In all, the attack siphoned 233.46 million XRP, a form of crypto, from five wallets into the hacker’s wallets, and then plundered other forms of crypto including bitcoin, in what may well have been the most lucrative heist of all time.
The culprits remain unclear. The FBI immediately blamed a notorious North Korean hacking outfit, but Pyongyang has denied involvement. Binance, in its report, noted that it had thwarted “57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases” — up until the big one that breached their defenses, at least.

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted.
But Leo XIV is forging ahead with a grueling 12-day visit, which includes Uruguay, Argentina, and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades.
He plans to cover a lot of ground – around 19,000 miles – while in Latin America. From November 6 to 17, the pope is scheduled to take 14 flights (including two in a helicopter), give 36 speeches and participate in around 50 events in what is one of the most intense papal trips of recent years.
He will also visit Cusco, Peru, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea-level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath. During the whole trip, he’ll travel to 10 cities, preside at large open-air Masses and vigils and meet with political leaders.
The trip, especially Cusco’s altitude, has raised questions about his health and the precautions being taken while there. It has also shone a light on a region that has profoundly shaped him and set his path to the papacy.
The pontiff had surgery last month to remove a third of his right lung after a small growth was discovered during routine checks, which was later confirmed as cancer. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said afterward that there were “no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place,” and doctors have said he does not need further treatment.
Vatican officials told reporters that Pope Leo will have a medical team available to him for the trip but stressed that no special measures are being taken. “We’re speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health,” the Vatican spokesman said ahead of the visit.
He explained the pope will travel with the “ordinary medical assistance,” including doctors, nurses and an ambulance, which usually travels with the pope’s convoy. But the spokesman said he wasn’t going into too much detail as the pope does not have a “permanent condition.” And if the Vatican medical team needs any help, one of the journalists traveling with the pope is also a doctor.
Montse Alvarado, the new head of Vatican Communications, told journalists on Tuesday that the pope’s “stamina is fantastic,” and that “he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen.”
Dr. Matthew Triplette, a pulmonologist from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, told CNN the risk of a medical emergency during the trip is “low” but that this could include “either a collapsed lung or blood clots.”
Triplette said the pope may be advised to “take low-dose blood thinners or use exercises or compression devices” to lower the possibility of blood clots in his legs when flying, which could cause major issues if they spread to the lungs. He added that the pope may feel more fatigue with exertion, particularly because there is less oxygen available at altitude.
In the aftermath of his surgery, many speculated that the trip would be canceled.
“I must confess that, until just a few days ago, I was among the few who had serious doubts about whether this trip could even take place,” Guzmán Carriquiry, a Uruguayan former Vatican official who worked on Latin American issues for nearly 50 years in the church’s central administration, told reporters on Tuesday.
But he also pointed out that the pope’s health team gave him the green light. “This suggests that his doctors believe the pope possesses a robust physical constitution; it also serves as a testament to the pope’s ardent desire and determination to go out and meet our people,” he said.
But Carriquiry noted that he would have removed Cusco from the agenda if he had organized the trip.
While Leo XIV is known for his gentle, low-key style, he is determined.
Answering a question from CNN, Alvarado said the pope “personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” and that he was looking forward to returning to Latin America.
The continent, and Peru in particular, is close to his heart, and Alvarado said the pope would speak off the cuff frequently in Spanish, a language he is fluent in.
“He’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go,” is how Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican foreign minister, put it at an event in Rome at the end of last month.
The Peruvian part of the trip will be emotional, as Leo arrives there “as an adopted brother, adopted by the Peruvian people,” said Carriquiry.
The pope, who remains a Peruvian citizen, had three stints in Peru, having first arrived there in his 30s. He also served as Bishop of Chiclayo in the northwest part of the country from 2015 to 2023.
The pope will return to Chiclayo during the trip and is expected to receive a rapturous welcome. Leo is remembered fondly in the city, where he was considered a hands-on bishop who was known to travel across his diocese on horseback.
“The pope spent many years living amongst the simple, poor and devout people of rural Latin America in northern Peru, as a missionary and a pastor,” Carriquiry, who is the former secretary of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, said.
Leo is expected to draw huge crowds when he’s there, with estimates of around 1.2 million people expected to attend his final Mass of the trip at Las Palmas Airbase in Lima.
He is also expected to draw huge crowds in Argentina, where more than a million people are expected to attend his Mass in Buenos Aires.
The late Pope Francis, the first Argentine pontiff, never made a visit to his home country, so Leo’s visit is one that is generating intense interest.
Francis never gave a clear reason as to why he didn’t visit Argentina. Carriquiry, a close friend of the late pope, said it “remains an enigma.”
Leo XIV’s visit will underline his plans to continue the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Argentine President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
Both Milei and Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori are notable figures in Latin America’s right-wing surge. They also enjoy support from the Trump administration, which Leo has publicly disagreed with — particularly on migration issues.
Leo XIV would not have been elected pope had he not been sent to Peru as a young Augustinian missionary.
His time in Latin America put him on a path to be spotted by Pope Francis. It was Francis who appointed the then-Rev. Robert Prevost as bishop in Chiclayo before later bringing him to Rome and naming him a cardinal.
All of this set him up as a candidate in the 2025 conclave. While Leo is the first pope from the United States and grew up in Chicago, his experience in Latin America has profoundly influenced his outlook.
In Peru, he served in the birthplace of liberation theology, a movement focused on social and political action to help the poor and oppressed. As a bishop, he was known for organizing practical assistance for those affected by floods or in need of medical equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic.
He served in a church in Peru which emphasized an inclusive model, giving greater roles to those not ordained as priests and bishops, including women.
Leo’s time in Peru also saw him exposed to the fallout of the clerical abuse crisis, including a major scandal involving a powerful Catholic group . The Vatican says the pope will have two meetings with abuse survivors during his trip, one in Argentina and another in Peru.

articles.title_orig: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.title_zh: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.content_orig:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

articles.title_orig: Will New Zealand Join Voters’ Global Revolt Over Soaring Costs?
articles.title_zh: Will New Zealand Join Voters’ Global Revolt Over Soaring Costs?
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand is set for one of its tightest elections in years, with the incumbent conservative coalition facing an uncertain path to power and polls pointing to a millennial newcomer becoming the kingmaker.
Support for two parties that have dominated Wellington politics for almost a century – the center-right National party and center-left Labour party – has cratered below 30% respectively in public polling, with voters turning to players entrenched further to the right, the left, and to a centrist party that could enter parliament for the first time.
Frustrated with soaring living costs, stubbornly high unemployment and a stagnant economy in recent years, voters on Saturday are looking beyond their traditional choices.
Shaking up the race is the centrist Opportunity party, led by Qiulae Wong, an articulate 38-year-old former sustainable business consultant and mother of two, who goes by ‘Q’ for short. She entered politics just a year ago by responding to a job advertisement for the party’s leadership role.
Her party, pitching itself as both business- and climate-friendly and promising a land tax as well as a universal basic income to replace welfare payments, looks set to secure enough votes to cross the 5% threshold required to secure seats in parliament, on current polling.
That would make it the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to do so in 30 years – a “super significant” feat according to Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Wellington’s Victoria University.
“There’s not been really anything like it, and we’ve seen a number of well-funded attempts,” she told CNN, explaining that the party was finding appeal with people “frustrated with the status quo.”
If Saturday’s results mirror the polls, Opportunity would hold the balance of power – with both the incumbent right and the opposition left coalition groupings in need of their support to secure a majority.
Effectively, that means Wong could have her choice of government, and her party is happy to work with either side.
But Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the right-wing National-led coalition government, has already ruled out a post-election deal with Opportunity. He may yet face the stark choice of walking that back or losing power.
Neither Luxon, who faced down two caucus confidence votes on his leadership this year, nor his key opponent Labour’s Chris Hipkins (a former prime minister himself) have been able to endear themselves to the public like former leaders Jacinda Ardern and John Key.
Their relative unpopularity has shattered a decades-long trend of battle royale-style campaigns between the major party leaders, giving the minor party contenders more attention and putting them in a position to have significant influence over the direction of the next government.
Coalitions are a near constant under the South Pacific nation’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, but the minor parties have traditionally been supporting players, granted a tiny proportion of cabinet posts and limited policy concessions.
The powerful position the minor parties find themselves in this year is “unprecedented territory,” says Greaves. “This is going to be the first time we’re going to see these coalition agreements where the minor parties are really going to be saying: ‘Hey, we got a big chunk of the vote. You have to stop treating us like children.’”
But that makes it “really hard to know what you’re voting for,” she said, explaining that fringe policies that get little attention during the campaign can ultimately end up on the government’s agenda after negotiations.
The incumbent National-led coalition – New Zealand’s most right-wing government in a generation – could be pushed further to the right by its emboldened partners, who have touted deepening culture war-style policies at times on the campaign trail.
For example, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party has vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while the nationalist New Zealand First party has promised sweeping immigration changes and its populist leader Winston Peters has voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy.
“With the 2023 government, a lot of people argue that that was already a huge lurch to the right, especially in terms of (indigenous) Māori rights … So that’s potentially concerning for more moderate voters,” said Greaves.
Conversely, parties on the right have warned voters would face a raft of new taxes if a leftist coalition were able to form a government – with Labour promising a capital gains tax, and the leftist Greens touting taxes on the “super rich” and big tech companies who take New Zealand-earned profits overseas.
“If the left bloc were to win, they would have this real concern about exactly how they get the money to do what they want to do,” said Greaves.
In recent decades, New Zealand elections have typically been easy to predict, but even the experts are struggling to foresee what voters will deliver on Saturday.
“What’s going to happen? No idea,” said Greaves.
Should Luxon’s National-led coalition lose, it will become the first single-term New Zealand government in more than half a century.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.title_zh: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.content_orig:
The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.
Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada
The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada .
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:
The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.
In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.
Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January .
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
articles.title_zh: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
articles.content_orig:
US Vice President JD Vance’s reported bid to meet Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei for peace talks with Tehran raises a troubling question for Washington: Does it understand the man it would face across the table?
For more than four decades, Rezaei has occupied positions of power from which he could make decisions that imposed extraordinary human and economic losses on Iranians, while he and his factional allies in the Islamic Republic remained largely insulated from their consequences.
Understanding this track record and how he calculates the costs of diplomacy is essential to understanding how he might negotiate with Washington, how much he is prepared to tolerate, and what could finally persuade him to compromise.
The origins of Rezaei’s cost-benefit calculus go back to 1981, when the founder of the Islamic Republic, Ruhollah Khomeini, appointed the 27-year-old Rezaei as commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The IRGC was at the time a newly established institution in which revolutionary commitment and willingness to sacrifice often carried greater weight than professional military judgment.
Rezaei flourished in that environment and, in turn, helped consolidate a command culture that treated heavy casualties as an acceptable cost of pursuing ideological or factional objectives. The relationship was mutually reinforcing, as the institution rewarded commanders willing to endure enormous losses, while those commanders perpetuated a system in which the political consequences of those losses rarely affected the people responsible for them.
That high threshold for enduring costs paid by others became particularly consequential in 1982, after Iranian forces recaptured the city of Khorramshahr and Iraq subsequently offered negotiations. As IRGC commander, Rezaei was among those who argued for entering Iraqi territory rather than halting at the border. A war begun by Saddam Hussein's invasion now became another six years of bloody battles for goals extending beyond Iran's capacity.
During the catastrophic Operation Ramadan near the port city of Basra in July 1982, Iranian troops, including forces under Rezaei's IRGC command, repeatedly attacked entrenched Iraqi positions. Historians Anthony H. Cordesman and Abraham R. Wagner estimate between 20,000 and 30,000 Iranian troops were killed or critically wounded. Some Iranian leaders nevertheless saw progress in exhausting Iraq.
One of my uncles was killed in Operation Ramadan, and another in the offensive campaigns Rezaei had advocated after Khorramshahr. In this calculation, a battlefield disaster became an investment in a hypothetical victory in the long run. That victory never came.
Iranian forces did improve tactically, as a US National Defense University study demonstrates in its account of the successful 1986 assault on Iraq’s Faw Peninsula. Yet those improvements rarely prompted Iranian commanders to reconsider whether their objectives justified the mounting human suffering and material losses, allowing the same strategic mistakes to persist even as battlefield methods evolved.
Later that year, Operation Karbala-4 proceeded despite warnings that Iraqi forces anticipated the assault and that the operation had been exposed. Thousands of mostly Iranian youths were killed, wounded or went missing. Decades afterward, Rezaei called the operation a “diversion” preceding Operation Karbala-5, before acknowledging that it began as a principal attack.
Here was another early expression of a dangerous institutional habit among Iranian decision-makers: a battlefield defeat could be treated as an investment in eventual victory, regardless of whether that victory was becoming more attainable or not.
The following year, Iranian forces continued operations toward Iraq’s Basra. A 2009 US National Defense University study, based on extensive interviews with former Iraqi Republican Guard commander Ra'ad Hamdani, described the fighting as the "Somme of the Iran-Iraq War," recalling frontal assaults with high casualties, enormous artillery concentrations and extraordinary destruction.
The National Defense University researchers concluded that repeated attacks reflected Iran’s persistent unwillingness to learn from previous failures. By 1987, they observed, Iranian political and military leaders were struggling to motivate soldiers who had suffered heavy losses without any meaningful gains.
Rezaei’s demands in the final year of the Iraq war exposed the deeper problem with his leadership style. In 1988, Rezaei set out requirements for rebuilding Iran’s offensive capacity over the following five years, including 350 infantry brigades, 2,500 tanks and 300 combat aircraft, while Prime Minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi’s government warned it could no longer finance the war.
Rezaei merely counted the weapons necessary for victory without offering a comparable accounting of the human cost of continuing the war. Ruhollah Khomeini accepted a ceasefire, and Rezaei remained commander until 1997.
Peace brought Rezaei new positions and privileges, but the wartime mentality that allowed him to accept enormous costs borne by others followed him into politics. He served as secretary of Iran's Expediency Council from 1997 to 2021 and expanded his influence beyond the military.
He ran unsuccessfully for president in 2009, 2013 and 2021, but those electoral defeats did little to diminish his access to senior positions within the Islamic Republic.
A Tehran Bureau investigation identified him as the owner of Tabnak, a major news website whose corporate structure included relatives and associates. He now had assets and networks worth protecting, even as he continued to regard sacrifice by others as an acceptable price for pursuing political objectives.
Rezaei’s response to his son’s dissent also illustrated the tension between family ties and political loyalty. Ahmad Rezaei had publicly criticized the Islamic Republic and fled the country. Mohsen Rezaei denounced him and declared that he would be treated like any dissident if he returned. Ahmad subsequently returned to Iran in 2005 and was not prosecuted, before leaving the country again.
Ahmad was found dead in Dubai in 2011. Police reported an apparent suicide, although questions persisted. Nevertheless, Rezaei's public response to his son's dissent suggested that even family ties could be subordinated to his position in a political order he had devoted his career to building.
In peacetime economic policy, the same institutional tolerance for high costs borne by Iranian citizens found another arena. Rezaei carried his understanding of costs into economics. Former associates of his presidential campaigns told me he conceived what became slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei's "resistance economy" and brought the idea to him.
As vice president for economic affairs under President Ebrahim Raisi from August 2021 to June 2023, he helped direct economic policy amid inflation and declining purchasing power. Once again, ordinary people financed the "resistance," while Rezaei retained his position and influence.
In an interview for this article, former Kayhan editor-in-chief and representative of Ali Khamenei Mehdi Nasiri alleged that Rezaei sought a share of Tehran’s roughly €2 billion electric-vehicle procurement deal with China under hardline Mayor Alireza Zakani in 2024, but declined to elaborate on the basis for his allegation. Separately, investigative journalist Yashar Soltani reported that the deal bypassed standard procurement procedures and involved intermediaries whose selection and financial qualifications were unclear. His report did not name Rezaei.
In August 2026, Rezaei became secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, returning to decisions over war and diplomacy. The body, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, coordinates Iran's security and foreign policy. articles.title_orig: Companies urged to adapt as restaurant franchisee files for bankruptcy: 'Businesses want to make excuses'
articles.title_zh: Companies urged to adapt as restaurant franchisee files for bankruptcy: 'Businesses want to make excuses'
articles.content_orig:
Entrepreneur Marcus Lemonis discusses voters' feelings about their finances and taxing millionaires following the midterm elections on 'Fox & Friends.'
Companies operating in California and across the nation face growing pressure to adapt to high overhead and point to local economic conditions as the reason for financial collapse, experts say.
"A lot of businesses want to make excuses now," entrepreneur and FOX Business contributor Marcus Lemonis said Friday during an appearance on "Fox & Friends."
"What I say to business owners, small, medium and large. … ‘These are the cards we are dealt. You’re going to have to make difficult decisions.'"
MCDONALD'S DEALT LEGAL SETBACK AS JUDGE ALLOWS MCRIB MEAT LAWSUIT TO PROCEED
Lemonis noted that many companies continue to thrive in the Golden State despite high costs and strict oversight.
"If the country is going to survive the way we want it to and prosper, we're going to have to run good businesses, regardless of what state we're in," he added.
An Outback Steakhouse franchisee with 61 restaurants is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy amid piling debt, citing soaring labor costs and inflation in California. (Joshua Lott/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Lemonis' remarks were in response to a question about San Diego–based Out West Restaurant Group, an Outback Steakhouse franchisee that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while pointing to California’s labor expenses and inflation as the primary catalyst for its distress.
Out West, officially known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, is seeking relief from a massive $449 million debt load. The company operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations across California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, a decline from the 99 restaurants it managed at its peak in 2018.
In court filings, CEO David Goronkin blamed a shrinking customer base and high operational overhead. California’s minimum wage hit $19.60 per hour in January. The filing also cited beef price increases of up to 5% annually since 2022.
"By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged," Goronkin stated in court documents. "Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise."
MCDONALD'S HIT WITH LAWSUIT CLAIMING MCRIB CONTAINS NO REAL RIB MEAT
Out West, officially known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, is seeking relief from a massive $449 million debt load. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
While sit-down restaurant chains were exempt from California's $20-per-hour fast-food minimum wage law passed in 2024, full-service restaurants have faced higher labor costs statewide.
To navigate its Chapter 11 restructuring, Out West is seeking court authorization to sell its assets.
"There's a cause and effect for everything," Lemonis said. "Either I'm going to raise the prices, I'm going to cut my staff (or) I'm gonna have to close. There's always a cause and effect, and I think what these DSA candidates are gonna realize quickly is the effect is going to actually impact the people that voted for them."
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Parent company Bloomin' Brands, which owns several restaurant chains, has agreed to purchase the remaining 61 Outback locations for $26.3 million.
The Florida-based parent company is also providing up to $5.5 million in interest-free debtor-in-possession financing.
FOX Business' Bradford Betz contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.title_zh: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The US added 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past economists' expectations, as the labor market showed strength despite the Federal Reserve's recent rate hikes.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% even amid a slight increase in labor force participation. September's underwhelming jobs report of 29,000 additions was also revised upward to a gain of 60,000 jobs.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, deemed the results "a blowout" in a post on X .
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg projected a gain of about 70,000 jobs in October and saw the unemployment rate holding steady. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September, better than expectations for 0.3% month-over-month growth. Annual earnings rose 3.1%, beating expectations but likely still below the current inflation rate.
Employers added jobs in a number of sectors of the economy. Professional and business services, which had been seen as more vulnerable to AI-related disruptions, added 70,000 roles. Healthcare, long a strong spot for job growth, added a higher-than-average 42,000 positions.
Transportation and warehousing jobs rose by 25,000, and manufacturing continued to show strength with 19,000 additions.
"This is still a low-hire, low-fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement.
Other job market measures released earlier this week telegraphed steady hiring — though not to the extent of Friday's report blowout number. Job openings and hiring edged higher , the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed; private employers added 86,000 jobs , according to ADP; and layoff plans dropped to a three-year low while seasonal hiring ramped up.
"Consistent with prior, more partial indicators of the US labor market, the October Jobs Report came in very strong, across the board," Wharton economist Mohamed El-Erian posted on X.
The solid report will likely give the Federal Reserve more confidence to move forward with another rate hike in December . The central bank will also consider November jobs data and October's inflation figures before its Dec. 9 rate decision. Traders currently see a 77% chance of a 25 basis point rate hike next month, up from 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch.
"Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.title_zh: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.content_orig:
Captains who wish to transit the Bab al-Mandab Strait have been using a communication channel with the Iran-backed Houthi terror group via email for safe transit, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
While technically the Houthis have said ships not linked to the US, UK, or Israel are allowed through the strait, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, shippers have begun emailing the terror group to receive assurances of their safety.
Emails are sent to an administrative entity established by the Houthis in early 2024 called the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, which handles applications and communicates the Houthis actions.
Emails seen by the WSJ show vessels stating that neither the ship nor the crew has any connections with Israel, the US, or the UK.
Ships will share their estimated schedules and assure that they will adhere to the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.
If the Houthis reply, they will typically do so within the next 24 hours, the WSJ wrote, citing crew members and emails.
In one instance, the Houthis sent authorization to the Chinese containership Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, issuing it a one-week permit and telling it to keep its Automatic Identification System, which broadcasts a ship's identity, position, speed, and destination, in operation through transit.
Additionally, the ship was told to keep VHF Channel 16, a marine VHF radio frequency designated as an international distress frequency, in operation.
The email ends with an invitation to call the HOCC hotline number if needed and to subscribe to the HOCC email alert service to receive news and updates from the Houthis.
The official guidance from international maritime authorities is that vessels should not engage or register with the HOCC, and many vessels choose not to contact them, the WSJ wrote.
However, the captain of the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling told the WSJ that the ship management told him to contact the Houthis as an extra precaution.

articles.title_orig: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.title_zh: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks in the U.S. steadied Friday after suffering one of their worst routs in years, as investors weighed the prospect of an AI investment slowdown resulting from Democratic midterm victories against the sector’s long-term growth potential.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 closed up 1.1% after plunging 6.3% on Thursday, its worst single-day performance since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The broader S&P 500 finished 0.3% higher, after tanking 4.4% Thursday, a drop that wiped out $2.8 trillion worth of wealth on paper.
A strong October jobs report Friday morning increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next policy meeting in December. The prospect of higher borrowing costs helped to push stocks down from their highs earlier in the day.
Investors continue to digest the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which a crop of Democratic candidates were elected to office who had pledged to rein in AI and data centers . They include Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a state that is among the largest data center markets in the country.
The AI boom is responsible for an ever-increasing share of U.S. stock market gains and economic growth, so any threat to the narrative of demand-fueled growth can rattle investors.
“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News.
The incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could also tighten scrutiny of the AI industry, including its infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs.
This would add to existing worries investors already have about the long-term profitability of these investments.
Some analysts viewed Thursday’s dramatic sell-off as overblown —  merely a sign of some froth coming off an overstretched market —  rather than the end of the line for the AI investment boom.
Recent declines are “just speed bumps,” said economist and investor Ed Yardeni.
Rather than spelling doom for the sector, Yardeni said losses like this week’s could ultimately help keep the AI bubble from overheating.
Until it becomes clearer how much data center construction is truly threatened by newly elected lawmakers, volatility is likely to continue.
“This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade, which is grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections,” said Alex Guiliano, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Resonate Wealth Partners.
Friday kicked off with steep losses in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020, falling as much as 6% and more than 20% since its most recent high, putting it in bear-market territory. South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.
The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are linked to the global AI spending cycle and “hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC chief market strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.
The months leading up to the American elections had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
In China, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”
That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.
“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_zh: The Duo apps are coming, says Apple
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch. But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front. The company on Friday announced there are now over 100,000 apps built for the Duo live on the App Store, and it’s seeing thousands more being added to the store every day.
The news was timed alongside the release of over a dozen more notable Duo-ready apps, including Microsoft Word and Outlook, Zoom, sports apps from the NBA and NHL, shopping apps like Etsy and LTK, productivity apps like Goodnotes and Extra, the Halide Mark III camera app, and others. These join the iPhone Duo-optimized apps that were already available, like Netflix, YouTube, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
Non-optimized apps are definitely less than ideal, as they come with a black bar on the side of the screen, which takes up valuable space. Sometimes, they hide important functions under an overflow menu.
Apple’s data seems to suggest that at least some iOS developers may have needed extra time to get their apps ready for its latest form factor. The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide. Here, the developers could use the Duo and work on their apps with Apple’s support.
The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year. On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve .
“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.
Other notable apps that have been updated for iOS 27 and optimized for the iPhone Duo include the following: Spotify, CBS, Tubi, BBC iPlayer (U.K.), Yahoo Fantasy Sports, Sportsnet (Canada), Facebook Messenger, Google Chat, ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Microsoft Copilot, Excel, PowerPoint, SAP Concur, monday.com, PDF Expert, Documents, iA Writer, Substack, The Washington Post, Yahoo News, FOX News, Kalshi, Yahoo Finance, Canva, Suno, Tinder, Google Translate, Strava, Alma, Withings, MyFitnessPal, Bevel, Transit, Citi Bike, ParkMobile, Viator, Tesla Robotaxi, Priceline, Kroger, Domino’s, Taco Bell, Untappd, The Weather Channel, FOX Weather, and RainViewer.
Not all these updates have yet to fully roll out, we should note.
Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo. However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

articles.title_orig: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
articles.title_zh: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions
articles.content_orig:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments
Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.
According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.
With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money.
The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. The men allegedly stole nearly $5m from a hospital system headquartered in Missouri; about $2.7m from a Rhode Island bank, about $3m from a California hospital system, over $4.6m from a mutual fund headquartered in Massachusetts and about $5m from a pet food company in Florida. The men also stole over $11m from a UK tech company.
The men would direct employees to wire money to bank accounts all over the world including in the United States, Spain , Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China. After the money had been wired, the men would covert the money into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distributed it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators”, according to the DoJ press release. Soall and Hazan went by several aliases: Soal’s nicknames included “Seba Clarke” and “Rocky Balboa,” while Hazan went by “Superman Cash,” “Fat Boy,” and “Ron.”
In a statement, Jamie McDonald, a US attorney, said artificial intelligence had great potential but that the public should recognize that some may seek to use the technology to pursue criminal goals.
“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large-scale fraud,” said James C Barnacle Jr, the FBI assistant director in charge, in a statement. “As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities.”
The men have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, various counts of money-laundering conspiracy and aggravated identity theft.
