articles.title_orig: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: How Elon Musk Frittered Away Nearly $500 Million on the Midterm Elections
articles.title_zh: How Elon Musk Frittered Away Nearly $500 Million on the Midterm Elections
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections.
The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close.
Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world.
Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported.
Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races .
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop."
Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities.
Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas.
SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings .
Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote.
Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia.
Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first.
SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
articles.title_zh: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
articles.content_orig:
watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.
If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.
Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:
Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.
It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.
This article isn’t about making the privacy case for the feature. You can read Apple’s privacy protections here . Briefly though, key details include: there’s no speaker attribution or logging of sensitive information like financial data, authentication data, or personal identifiers; no audio is stored or recorded; the feature is opt-in; and you can set times or places where it stays disabled.
Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.
I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.
Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.
One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.
Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.
It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.
What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Investors brace for lower Anthropic valuation, calling $1.5 trillion a 'stretch'
articles.title_zh: Investors brace for lower Anthropic valuation, calling $1.5 trillion a 'stretch'
articles.content_orig:
Following tech's selloff on Wall Street this week, some investors are lowering their expectations for Anthropic.
The artificial intelligence company had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO up until recently, but stakeholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch."
Anthropic declined to comment.
The change in sentiment comes alongside growing concerns about the outsized spending by AI companies and a sharp post-midterm slump in the market. The Nasdaq plummeted more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months, reflecting fears that Democrats' newfound power in Washington, D.C., and a nationwide rebuke of AI will lead to a slowdown in the buildout of data centers.
Bearishness on the AI trade was on the rise before the election. The Nasdaq suffered its worst month in October since March 2025, led by declines in chipmakers and neoclouds.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq , under the ticker ANT, and is gearing up for an expected debut in a matter of weeks. Last month, Anthropic was reportedly seeking a valuation as high as $2 trillion . As of May, the company was privately valued at $965 billion.
With the latest market turmoil, one investor said $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion is a more likely valuation target, although that could change with market conditions. The investors asked not to be named because they're not authorized to speak about the matter.
Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC that, "Investors will expect the IPO to be priced at least at the low end of previous expectations."
"The market really needs this IPO to go well and the bankers on the deal surely understand that," Luria said. "The best way to set Anthropic up for success is to price the deal well."
The company is expected to kick off its roadshow next week.

articles.title_orig: Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
articles.title_zh: Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian citizen of Israel casts her ballot in the country's general election at a polling station in Umm al-Fahm, Israel, Oct. 27, 2026 Mahmoud Illean/AP hide caption
KUFR QASI, Israel — In recent years many Palestinian citizens of Israel shunned elections, believing there was little to gain from participating in the politics of a state which, they say, regularly marginalizes their communities and oppresses their fellow Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
But last month, Palestinian Arabs in Israel came to the ballot boxes in record numbers, helping strip Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's most far-right government in Israel's history of its majority, and giving Arab-led parties the votes they needed to become a powerful force in Israeli politics.
"We blocked the government of Netanyahu from continuing," said Jamal Zahalka, chairman of the High Follow-Up Committee, the main umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. "It's a historical achievement. I think our community found its strength."
Neither Netanyahu's coalition, nor his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot's center-right opposition, reached the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government. Arab-led parties won 19 out of 120 seats — enough to give them a critical role in the negotiations that will now determine who governs Israel at this turbulent moment in the country's history.
The election results strike at the heart of the decades-long questions about how Israel defines itself and the role of Palestinian Arabs in its society.
At a park in the Palestinian-majority town of Kufr Qasim two days after the election, hundreds of people gathered for the annual commemoration of residents gunned down in 1956 by Israeli border police on the opening day of the Suez Crisis in the violent early years of the state, when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal.
"And today we stand here, 70 years later," the speaker told the large crowd from a podium: "And the story still isn't over."
The crowd at this event, mostly dressed in black — some wearing the keffiyeh, the black and white stitched scarf symbolizing Palestinian resistance — mourned not only their lost relatives all those years ago, but also the suffering of Palestinians now: the sharp rise in discrimination against their communities in Israel since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023; Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left a population to survive amid the ruins of the enclave. And the actions of Netanyahu's extreme right-wing government in the occupied West Bank, where rights groups and the U.N. say it has armed and supported settlers as they force Palestinians from their homes and agricultural lands with unprecedented violence.
Worsening rights inside Israel was one reason, residents of Kufr Qasm told NPR, why so many Palestinian citizens in Israel went to the ballot boxes. "There is no freedom anymore," said Intisar Sarsur, 65, sitting with relatives beside an olive tree in the park in Kufr Qasim. " We are seeking for our basic rights as human beings."
"Everybody that I know participated in the elections. Not one person stayed home," Sarsur said. She and her family were sharing platters of mutabbaq , a sweet Palestinian layered pastry, and freshly pressed olive oil from this year's olive harvest — usually a joyous moment in the Palestinian calendar, that she said now felt bittersweet. This year the olive harvest for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank was marred by frequent attacks by Israeli settlers trying to disrupt this economically and culturally significant time of year.
Mansour Abbas, a lawmaker in Israel's parliament and leader of the conservative Muslim Ra'am party, embraces a supporter after the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Sakhnin, Israel, on Oct. 27. Mahmoud Illean/AP hide caption
Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of those who remained as the state of Israel was established in 1948 (when a majority of the prewar population was forcibly expelled or fled during the war) now make up about 20% of the population.
This election, Arab-led parties received a 64% increase in votes compared to the last elections, according to the Central Elections Committee. The gains they made have stirred anger, and even fear, among many on Israel's political right, who see them as a threat to the country's Jewish character.
Netanyahu and his allies made the large Arab turnout a rallying cry. On election day, Netanyahu posted a video calling it an "emergency." Itamar Ben Gvir, the far-right national security minister, filmed his own appeal at the entrance to Kufr Qasim: "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!"
As results came in, Netanyahu's Likud party went further. It claimed Arab parties had "stolen" the election through bribery, threats and forgery, and later warned of a foreign takeover of the Knesset and the "Islamization of Israel." The party has made no evidence public. Police say they found no basis for the claims, and election officials say there was no widespread fraud. The head of the elections committee separately asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate suspected foreign funding of efforts to boost Arab turnout. But he and the attorney general say the vote was conducted properly and the results were not compromised.
The messaging by Netanyahu's bloc is widely seen as an attempt to prevent Eisenkot's center-right grouping from partnering with Arab parties — a reality that would give Eisenkot the majority he needs to form a government. But the sharp rise in anti-Arab sentiment since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed, has made an alliance with any Arab party potentially politically treacherous and could cause other Jewish right wing members of his bloc to split off in fury.
Eisenkot is not a natural ally for Arab parties either. A former military chief of staff whose son was killed fighting in Gaza, he served as an observer in Netanyahu's war cabinet early in the war. And he still cuts a hawkish figure. As a general, he is credited with formulating the "Dahiyeh doctrine," which he laid out in 2008: using "disproportionate force" against villages from which militants fire on Israel, which he called "not civilian villages" but "military bases." It is named after Beirut's southern suburbs, a Hezbollah stronghold that Israel largely decimated in heavy bombardment in 2006.
Campaign billboards show the Ra'am party (left) and the Joint List of Arab-led parties in the Bedouin city of Rahat, southern Israel, Nov. 1. David Goldman/AP hide caption
So Arab parties are divided on how to use the power they gained in this election. Ra'am, a socially conservative Islamist party, campaigned on joining a governing coalition and put a Jewish former police official second on its list. But for now the Joint List alliance that won 11 of the 19 Arab-led party seats in this election won't formally partner with Eisenkot. Its leaders have said they could back his government from the outside, but won't join it, citing Israel's ongoing war in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.
President Isaac Herzog has been consulting with parties over who they would support to try to form a coalition. He is expected to announce which candidate he'll give a mandate to next week, to try to form a coalition. That candidate will have 28 days and can ask for a further two-week extension. If he fails, another candidate is given only 28 days (without extension) to try to form a government. And if no one manages to form a coalition, there will be repeat elections next year.
In Kufr Qasim, as the readings and re-enactments of the 1956 killings unfurled on stage, Mansour Shaaban said he would vote again in an instant. Aged 33, this was the first election he had voted in. But now he said it's necessary to try to stop what he ca

articles.title_orig: The final day of voting begins in New Zealand's election as an unusual law bans any talk of politics
articles.title_zh: The final day of voting begins in New Zealand's election as an unusual law bans any talk of politics
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand is set for one of its tightest elections in years, with the incumbent conservative coalition facing an uncertain path to power and polls pointing to a millennial newcomer becoming the kingmaker.
Support for two parties that have dominated Wellington politics for almost a century – the center-right National party and center-left Labour party – has cratered below 30% respectively in public polling, with voters turning to players entrenched further to the right, the left, and to a centrist party that could enter parliament for the first time.
Frustrated with soaring living costs, stubbornly high unemployment and a stagnant economy in recent years, voters on Saturday are looking beyond their traditional choices.
Shaking up the race is the centrist Opportunity party, led by Qiulae Wong, an articulate 38-year-old former sustainable business consultant and mother of two, who goes by ‘Q’ for short. She entered politics just a year ago by responding to a job advertisement for the party’s leadership role.
Her party, pitching itself as both business- and climate-friendly and promising a land tax as well as a universal basic income to replace welfare payments, looks set to secure enough votes to cross the 5% threshold required to secure seats in parliament, on current polling.
That would make it the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to do so in 30 years – a “super significant” feat according to Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Wellington’s Victoria University.
“There’s not been really anything like it, and we’ve seen a number of well-funded attempts,” she told CNN, explaining that the party was finding appeal with people “frustrated with the status quo.”
If Saturday’s results mirror the polls, Opportunity would hold the balance of power – with both the incumbent right and the opposition left coalition groupings in need of their support to secure a majority.
Effectively, that means Wong could have her choice of government, and her party is happy to work with either side.
But Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the right-wing National-led coalition government, has already ruled out a post-election deal with Opportunity. He may yet face the stark choice of walking that back or losing power.
Neither Luxon, who faced down two caucus confidence votes on his leadership this year, nor his key opponent Labour’s Chris Hipkins (a former prime minister himself) have been able to endear themselves to the public like former leaders Jacinda Ardern and John Key.
Their relative unpopularity has shattered a decades-long trend of battle royale-style campaigns between the major party leaders, giving the minor party contenders more attention and putting them in a position to have significant influence over the direction of the next government.
Coalitions are a near constant under the South Pacific nation’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, but the minor parties have traditionally been supporting players, granted a tiny proportion of cabinet posts and limited policy concessions.
The powerful position the minor parties find themselves in this year is “unprecedented territory,” says Greaves. “This is going to be the first time we’re going to see these coalition agreements where the minor parties are really going to be saying: ‘Hey, we got a big chunk of the vote. You have to stop treating us like children.’”
But that makes it “really hard to know what you’re voting for,” she said, explaining that fringe policies that get little attention during the campaign can ultimately end up on the government’s agenda after negotiations.
The incumbent National-led coalition – New Zealand’s most right-wing government in a generation – could be pushed further to the right by its emboldened partners, who have touted deepening culture war-style policies at times on the campaign trail.
For example, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party has vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while the nationalist New Zealand First party has promised sweeping immigration changes and its populist leader Winston Peters has voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy.
“With the 2023 government, a lot of people argue that that was already a huge lurch to the right, especially in terms of (indigenous) Māori rights … So that’s potentially concerning for more moderate voters,” said Greaves.
Conversely, parties on the right have warned voters would face a raft of new taxes if a leftist coalition were able to form a government – with Labour promising a capital gains tax, and the leftist Greens touting taxes on the “super rich” and big tech companies who take New Zealand-earned profits overseas.
“If the left bloc were to win, they would have this real concern about exactly how they get the money to do what they want to do,” said Greaves.
In recent decades, New Zealand elections have typically been easy to predict, but even the experts are struggling to foresee what voters will deliver on Saturday.
“What’s going to happen? No idea,” said Greaves.
Should Luxon’s National-led coalition lose, it will become the first single-term New Zealand government in more than half a century.

articles.title_orig: We Energies rate hike approved, customers to pay more in 2027 and 2028
articles.title_zh: We Energies rate hike approved, customers to pay more in 2027 and 2028
articles.content_orig:
Wisconsin regulators approved another rate increase, but the final impact on customers' monthly bills has yet to be determined.
Wisconsin regulators approved another rate increase, but the final impact on customers' monthly bills has yet to be determined.
We Energies customers will see their energy bills rise over the next two years after Wisconsin regulators approved a rate increase, though the final amount has not been determined.
Preliminary estimates were released on Friday after this report aired:
The Public Service Commission of Wisconsin, a nonpartisan, three-member board, met for more than 10 hours Thursday before voting on the request. It will be the energy company’s sixth rate increase since 2020.
In April, We Energies said its proposed rate changes would increase bills by about $13 per month in 2027 and another $8 to $9 per month in 2028. The PSC did not finalize the rates Thursday.
We Energies said the increase will support “key investments,” including more Wisconsin-produced energy, continued tree trimming to reduce power outages and the placement of power lines underground to strengthen the grid against severe weather.
“Our customers count on us every day for the energy they need, and we recognize our responsibility to continue providing safe and reliable energy, while keeping customer bills as low as possible,” a We Energies spokesperson said. “During this months-long process we worked with customer groups and Commission staff to reduce costs to customers by tens of millions of dollars.”
The Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, an independent nonprofit consumer advocacy group, expects the increase to be less than what We Energies requested.
“Based on where [the PSC] landed on key issues, we can say with confidence that this rate hike will be well below what the utility asked for,” said Tom Content, the group’s executive director. “The savings could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars, but unfortunately not enough to stop an increase from taking effect.”
The Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin echoed that assessment, saying that while reducing the requested increase was “a meaningful step toward holding the utility accountable and protecting customers from excessive costs,” the decision underscored the need for stronger protections against repeated increases and broader reform.
We Energies said that regardless of the final increase, Wisconsin energy costs will remain below the national average and in line with rates elsewhere in the Midwest.
The commission’s written order, which will include the final rates, is expected in a few weeks.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
articles.title_zh: Nvidia hardware worth $11.4M vanished between Oakland and Texas
articles.content_orig:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Authorities are investigating the theft of more than $11 million worth of Nvidia computer hardware in Oakland, in what experts describe as a sophisticated cargo heist targeting one of the world's most valuable technology companies.
According to reporting by the Bay Area News Group, the theft involved $11.4 million worth of Nvidia cargo that disappeared after departing Oakland on its way to Texas.
The shipment, consisting of six pallets of Nvidia hardware, left Oakland on Aug. 29 and was bound for Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities said the cargo was picked up as planned by a truck identified as a food transport company.
Investigators later lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County.
In a statement, Oakland police said: "The Oakland Police Department is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026."
Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business and has expertise in artificial intelligence, emerging technology and global economics, said Nvidia chips are highly sought after.
"There's lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak," Groth said.
He said the chips can command significantly higher prices outside the United States.
"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," Groth said.
The theft is the latest in a series of crimes targeting high-value technology shipments in the Bay Area. Last year, police in Fremont and Union City investigated burglaries involving Nvidia cargo valued at more than $7.5 million.
Groth said the scale and complexity of such thefts suggest increasingly sophisticated criminal operations.
"Because the cargoes are getting bigger. The heists are getting more complex and that will point toward a professionalization of the teams that are hijacking these," he said.
An ABC7 viewer also provided video of a separate attempted theft in September. According to police, suspects believed they were targeting trucks carrying expensive Nvidia technology. The trucks instead contained 40,000 pounds of sand.
Groth said the incidents highlight broader concerns about protecting advanced computing technology.
"Security has to get a lot tighter around these because they're a national security asset," he said.
He also raised concerns about where stolen hardware could ultimately end up.
"This is a national security concern as well because we don't know where these chips are going. They could be going to China, they could be anywhere where we have conflict in the world," Groth said.
Authorities have not announced any arrests in the $11.4 million theft, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Experts say the case underscores growing concerns about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security implications when advanced computer hardware enters the black market.

articles.title_orig: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.title_zh: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip with a first stop in secular Uruguay
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.title_zh: AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. The lone exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an added review of industrial projects, including data centers.
Ohio alone accounted for more than half of the measures, with 21 on the ballot. The issue also played out at the top of the ticket, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers."
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
Those plans could now run into resistance from the governor's mansion. Ohio's top office flipped blue on Tuesday, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the most significant results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying he put the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
The losses came despite record spending from Silicon Valley to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , the cycle’s largest individual donor, spent at least $474 million, nearly half of it in Texas, and lost both of the state’s marquee races. It was a warning sign for the wave of tech companies and founders who left California for Texas in search of a friendlier business climate.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the House Oversight Committee, summed it up in two words: "Lawyer up."
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: ChatGPT ‘manipulated and encouraged’ a woman in her plot to poison her husband, suit alleges
articles.title_zh: ChatGPT ‘manipulated and encouraged’ a woman in her plot to poison her husband, suit alleges
articles.content_orig:
A North Carolina man sued OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT gave his estranged wife detailed instructions on how to poison him.
James Gates, of Charlotte, said he fell severely ill in July 2025 but recovered. He later found a note handwritten by his wife, Cheryl Harris Gates, that referred to the plan and included a reminder to delete her ChatGPT history, the civil lawsuit says.
The suit, filed in October in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges the chatbot is “defective” and “manipulated and encouraged” Harris Gates to poison her husband. It says Gates suffers from severe physical and emotional harm.
An OpenAI spokesperson said “safety is a top priority” and that Harris Gates was banned from the platform. The company said it works with mental health experts to help ChatGPT recognize signs of distress and to expand access to localized crisis resources and hotlines.
Harris Gates was arrested in October 2025 and charged with attempted murder and contaminating food or drink with a controlled substance. The district attorney’s office later dropped the charges for lack of evidence.
An attorney for Harris Gates declined to comment.
According to the lawsuit, Harris Gates began using ChatGPT in early 2025  to assist with work evaluations. She was then employed by Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and her husband worked in cybersecurity.
By summer, the suit says, she relied heavily on the chatbot for children’s activities, gardening and appearance advice, and household questions. She eventually began sharing her frustrations about her marriage.
“During this same period the couple’s marriage had come under increasing strain, primarily driven by finances,” the suit says. The couple had discussed divorce, but Gates had not contacted a divorce attorney.
The lawsuit alleges ChatGPT validated Harris Gates’ frustrations and began “feeding Cheryl’s increasing mistrust and delusions about her husband spying on her and planning to leave her and her kids with nothing.” Gates had told his wife he never intended to do that, the suit says.
Over several conversations, Harris Gates allegedly portrayed her husband as “narcissistic” and “controlling.” She is also accused of asking for details “about how to poison her husband, including what dosages and drugs to use and combine for his weight,” and how to conceal the purchases from law enforcement.
In one exchange, the suit alleges, she asked about the toxic plant oleander and inquired about how many leaves would be lethal. She allegedly framed her questions “as self-protection,” saying she feared her husband would poison her with it. ChatGPT responded with specific instructions on preparation, dosage and administration, and whether the plant would show up on an autopsy, the suit alleges. It says the chatbot also told her the plant’s bitter taste could be masked in her husband’s energy drink.
In another exchange, the suit says, Harris Gates asked if mixing  Ambien and pregabalin “is better hidden in a beer at night or Celsius in the morning.” The chatbox allegedly said the energy drink would be better and then made a table “rating which drinks best mask the taste of the poisons.”
The suit further alleges she asked which combinations and doses of drugs already in the home could be made lethal, and that ChatGPT told her how to deliver them. It also alleges the chatbox named local places where she could anonymously buy castor beans, the main source of ricin.
During the July 2025 incident, Gates said, he had a racing heart, extreme jitteriness and uncontrollable shaking. His symptoms were so severe that he could not leave his couch for days, the suit says.
A month later, according to the suit, Gates recorded a video of himself pouring his energy drink into a cup after leaving it open on the kitchen counter while his wife was home. He wanted to see if anything was in it  but noticed nothing. The video was later given to police.
Gates told USA Today that his wife moved in August 2025. He said he found the handwritten note after she came to pick up her belongings and left a notebook on the kitchen counter. When he picked it up, the paper fell out.
The suit alleges that Harris Gates’ Amazon history showed searches for syringes. Liquid droppers, syringes, a scale and gloves were found at the home during a police search, it says. It also accuses ChatGPT of prompting her to delete her chat history so it cannot be accessed, even if subpoenaed.
Gates’ lawsuit says OpenAI was negligent and seeks unspecified damages. He told USA Today that he is separated from his wife and has temporary custody of the children.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The Taipei Mayor Election Is Not About China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
In October, well-known Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai, popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, was spotted by the media attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, a legislator running for mayor of Taipei. Given Tsai’s popularity in China, his appearance quickly sparked criticism. The incumbent Taipei mayor, Chiang Wan-an, helped defuse the controversy by inviting Tsai to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Three weeks after attending Shen’s campaign event, Tsai publicly stated that he had never supported Taiwanese independence and that his work required him to interact with people holding a range of political views. The following day, he attended Chiang’s campaign event.
If attending a rally is tantamount to declaring one’s support for Taiwan’s future, imagine what will be made of the November 28 vote.
Shen, the candidate of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has spent years studying Chinese influence operations and promoting civilian preparedness in Taiwan. Chinese authorities have opened an investigation into him on allegations of secession. Chiang, the Kuomintang (KMT) incumbent, has maintained an open channel of communication between officials in Taipei and Shanghai. Beijing and Washington may be tempted to interpret a Shen victory as a vote for independence or a Chiang victory as a turn toward China. Either interpretation, however, would link a municipal election to an issue that Taipei’s voters have not been asked to vote on.
Consider an exchange during the October 31 debate between Shen and Chiang. Chiang challenged Shen to explain why two redevelopment projects, one in Datong and the other in Neihu, had stalled. Chiang attributed the delays to restrictions on building heights near Taipei’s Songshan Airport. Shen fired back with a question of his own: If city officials knew about these restrictions, why hadn’t they explained them to residents from the outset? Chiang used the exchange to question his challenger’s command of city affairs. Shen, in turn, used it to ask what good that expertise did residents if they learned about an obstacle too late to do anything about it.
The most important takeaway from their heated exchanges, however, is not what the candidates said, but what they left unsaid. China, the elephant in the room when it comes to cross-strait relations, was not raised even once as a key issue during the two-hour debate.
That encapsulates the kind of local issues Taipei voters will actually base their decision on. Some might vote for Chiang, crediting him with moving other difficult projects forward, including one at Nanjichang Night Market. Others might favor Shen’s proposal to screen older buildings for earthquake risks and to help residents arrange repairs. Two homeowners could vote for different candidates – while holding precisely the same views about China. The election night count offers no way to tell.
Taipei’s recent electoral history illustrates the limits of interpreting local elections through the lens of national politics – and vice versa. In 2022, the city elected Chiang as mayor. Just over a year later, in the presidential election, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te carried Taipei, edging out the KMT’s Hou Yu-ih by just 641 votes. Chiang’s mayoral victory would therefore have been a poor guide to the city’s presidential preferences. There is even less reason to interpret a vote in the capital as evidence of a broader change of heart across Taiwan for or against a political party – or that party’s approach to China.
True, the result will shape national politics. Winning Taipei would give Shen a larger audience for his work on civilian defense. A second term would give Chiang greater standing within the KMT to make the case for engagement with Shanghai, and possibly Beijing. Plus, the Taipei mayorship has in the past served as a launching pad for presidential ambitions. Winning office gives a politician the chance to advance causes that may have had little to do with why voters chose him.
The election’s outcome could certainly also influence cross-strait relations. During Chiang’s tenure, the Taipei–Shanghai Twin-City Forum has kept officials from the two cities in contact. A Chiang victory would give him another term to pursue those exchanges. A Shen victory would test the conditions under which they can continue. Although Shen has criticized the forum’s value, he has said he would attend if it offered practical benefits and came without political preconditions. On October 14, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office dismissed his offer, citing his alleged support for independence.
Suppose Shen wins, repeats his offer, and finds Shanghai unwilling to meet with him. Concluding that Taipei voters chose to sever contact would erase Beijing’s role in the decision. The reverse inference – that vote for Chiang implies approval of his engagement with Chinese officials – would be equally questionable. A Taipei resident might value Chiang’s ability to keep municipal officials talking while still opposing closer political ties. Wanting the conversation with Shanghai to continue is entirely compatible with wanting Beijing to have less say in Taiwan’s affairs.
Local governance is undoubtedly important for the stability of the Taiwan Strait. Taipei’s city government, for example, helps residents prepare for an air raid, down to practicing how to reach shelter when the sirens sound. How well the city carries out that work matters regardless of which party holds power. Still, it’s not going to be an issue that is top of mind when Taipei residents fill out their ballots.
On November 28, Taipei’s voters will choose who takes responsibility for the safety of their homes, the city’s readiness for an emergency, and its dealings with Shanghai. Beijing and Washington have good reason to pay close attention to what the next mayor does with that authority. But anyone claiming a mandate for independence or unification is looking for evidence the mayoral count cannot provide.

articles.title_orig: The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years
articles.title_zh: The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of stunning ice age drawings discovered inside Spanish cave
The find includes 280 engravings, including 55 depictions of animals
By Jackie Flynn Mogensen edited by Claire Cameron
An engraving depicting a horse.
“Filling Gaps: The Palaeolithic Rock Art of the Cova de la Font Major on the North-east Iberian Peninsula,” by Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès, in Antiquity . Published online November 5, 2026
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
For decades, Cova de la Font Major has been a tourist destination in northeastern Spain. Despite all the visitors who have passed through the cave, only now are archaeologists revealing its secret: hundreds of stunning ice age rock engravings, including a rare depiction of a bear.
In a new study published in the journal Antiquity this week, researchers describe the discovery of 280 Paleolithic engravings at the large, underground cave in Espluga de Francolí, Spain. The cave was first excavated in 1957—since then thousands of people have likely been in it, and some even graffitied the walls without realizing they were disturbing ice age art, the researchers say.
The find is among the largest collections of cave art on the Iberian Peninsula. The engravings include 55 animal figures such as horses, deer and at least one bear, as well as less recognizable forms, such as parallel lines and an unusual group of loops.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Engravings of parallel lines ( top ) and loops ( bottom ).
“Filling Gaps: The Palaeolithic Rock Art of the Cova de la Font Major on the North-east Iberian Peninsula,” by Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès, in Antiquity . Published online November 5, 2026
It’s unclear how the engravings went so long without being noticed. In a dark cave, it may have been harder to spot the etchings than other forms of rock art such as paintings , says Míriam Salas-Altès, a co-author of the paper and a Ph.D. student at University of Rovira i Virgili and the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA), both in Spain.
Even wearing a helmet with a forward-facing light might not fully illuminate markings either. And the walls are “full” of graffiti, Salas-Altès says. To the untrained eye, Paleolithic engravings may have been difficult to differentiate from modern markings, she adds.
“Filling Gaps: The Palaeolithic Rock Art of the Cova de la Font Major on the North-east Iberian Peninsula,” by Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès, in Antiquity . Published online November 5, 2026
This type of cave art is also rare for this part of Spain. Before now, most Paleolithic cave art in the area has been found in the Franco-Cantabrian region, an area spanning the border of Spain and France. Just two cave figures had previously been found in Catalonia, Salas-Altès says.
“It was a big surprise,” she says.
Today tourists’ access to the cave has been limited to protect the engravings, which were first discovered in 2019.
Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, a researcher at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) in Spain, photographs the Paleolithic engravings at Gatoneres de Cal Palletes in Spain’s Cova de la Font Major.
Míriam Salas-Altès/IPHES-CERCA
Salas-Altès hopes to continue working to decipher the 280 engravings, as well as to understand the history of human presence in the cave. It’s unclear whether early humans used this cave simply for shelter, ritual practices or something else, she says.
And there may be more engravings to find—some galleries within Cova de la Font Major, for instance, have been filled with sediment over the years, Salas-Altès says, and opening them up could reveal even more rock art.
Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.

Our editors and reporters are often experts in their fields, which means they understand the nuances of big discoveries and can untangle the breakthroughs from the hype. With a subscription, you are also supporting rigorous fact-checking to ensure the words we publish are precise and accurate. And you’re supporting original illustrations, graphics and photos that bring you closer to an advanced laboratory, an ice sheet in Antarctica or a space mission in orbit. You’re helping us craft other types of high-quality journalism as well: Our newsletters are carefully written, edited and curated by staffers you have or will come to know and love. Our Science Quickly podcast is based on original reporting, collaboration with editors and scientists and exacting production.
Subscriptions keep this engine running so we can continue to deliver thoughtful, rigorous and independent science journalism to you. In an era of viral misinformation, this work is crucial. If you value what we do, I hope you’ll consider joining us as a subscriber

articles.title_orig: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
articles.title_zh: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
articles.content_orig:
A close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment checking the identification and traceability of blood samples beside a donor during a mobile blood donation session in Paimpol Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 23, 2026. Helene Rigny/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.
"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.
Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.
However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.
"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."
On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.
The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."
"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.
The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.
It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.
Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.
Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.
Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.
"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.
"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.
Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.
For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.
Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.
While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.
Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.
Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.
Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.
"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."
Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.
The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.

articles.title_orig: Anatomy of a Selloff: Sudden Chain Reaction Rattles Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Anatomy of a Selloff: Sudden Chain Reaction Rattles Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Retail traders dumped the most stocks in a single day since the Covid pandemic, amid Thursday's massive tech selloff, according to Vanda Research.
Retail investors sold a net $338 million of single stocks on Thursday, with not even an hour into the close, which the market research firm noted was the largest one-day outflow since March 2020 for a group that has been known to buy the dip and keep cash within the market.
The selling comes amid a massive stock market drawdown as traders rotated out of technology. On Thursday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average plummeted 1,800 points, effectively erasing any post-midterm bump, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped into a correction.
"On a typical sell-off, retail buy the dip," read a note from the firm. "Today, that bid has effectively disappeared from individual names."
The firm noted that what buying remained has been concentrated in leveraged vehicles such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ (TQQQ), which delivers three times the performance in the Nasdaq-100 index, and the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (SOXL), which is supposed to track moves in semiconductors.
"This looks like a rare buyers' strike colliding with forced selling," read the note.
— CNBC's Nick Wells contributed to this story.
(Correction: Fixes day of the week in first paragraph.)

articles.title_orig: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.title_zh: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe’s backlash spreads
articles.content_orig:
Protesters in the Netherlands have broken into a construction site for a new Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, the latest action in a growing movement sweeping Europe.
Several hundred activists occupied the site in the Sloterdijk district on Friday, responding to a call for a two-day protest across Europe against data centres, which handle the large processing workloads associated with artificial intelligence (AI). Demonstrators clashed with police as some climbed a crane and set off flares.
Nathan Timmer, of the protest group Geef Tegengas – which translates as Push Back – told local broadcaster AT5 that demonstrators were occupying the site in an effort to stop construction.
“We don’t want it to be built. Nobody needs it,” Timmer said. “The only thing this will be used for is AI slop. AI warfare, data surveillance and committing genocide. We don’t want that.”
Pro-Palestinian activists also joined the demonstrations in the Dutch capital. By late afternoon police were escorting activists off the construction site, though some remained, local media reported.
Dutch police said they detained 150-200 people suspected of trespassing during the protest.
Microsoft said it was aware of the Amsterdam demonstration.
“We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully,” a spokesperson said. “However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
Data centres face resistance around the world due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use. Activists argue that the boom in facilities serving cloud computing and AI is moving faster than public consultation and environmental oversight.
Dozens of civil society and grassroots groups have said they will join the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday in 15 European countries, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom, organisers said.
In Germany, a dozen protesters gathered in front of a data centre on the outskirts of Berlin on Friday.
“We want to put a stop to this blind construction of data centres around Germany, regardless of any environmental concerns,” said protest spokeswoman Caro Weber. “This is really, really dangerous for our future.”
About 100 people also protested against data centres in front of the Polish parliament, representing communities around Warsaw where new centres are planned.
In Italy, the fast-growing data centre industry is facing an equally rapid rise in grassroots opposition, particularly in the northern Lombardy region, the country’s main hub for digital infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Terrifying moment woman intervenes in bush struggle between koala and python
articles.title_zh: Terrifying moment woman intervenes in bush struggle between koala and python
articles.content_orig:
A Brisbane wildlife rescuer has saved a baby koala from the deadly grip of a python after coming across the pair while out for a bushwalk.
Nell was walking her dog in Whites Hill Reserve at Camp Hill, when she heard a commotion, about 15 metres off the footpath.
"I heard a lot of birds, so I ran over and that's when I saw the joey look me dead in the eyes panicked and the mum was scratching at a python as she tried to get it off her baby."
"She was really distressed," she said.
That's when Nell jumped into action and scooped up the joey, before she started to unravel the snake.
"I didn't know if the baby was breathing or had broken ribs or anything in that moment, I just picked it up and started unravelling," Nell said.
The koala and the cub embraced after the rescue. ( Supplied: @behappy.golucky )
"It all happened so quickly … and all of a sudden I've got the snake in one hand and then the joey clutching onto my left shoulder crying."
The rescuer said a man walking nearby stopped to offer his help but was not thrilled when she tried to hand over the snake.
She said she asked him to hold the snake, but he very quickly said no and offered to hold her dog instead.
Nell said she put the snake into a small tree while she checked the freed joey for injuries before reuniting it with mum who had stayed close by throughout the ordeal.
"I made sure its limbs were moving correctly and that it was breathing ok … then I walked up to the tree that its mum was in and it went straight up to her."
Nell was walking with her dog Pluto when they saw the koala in the snake's clutches. ( Supplied: @behappy.golucky )
"I then walked with the snake wrapped around my arm until I felt it was far enough that it wasn't going to come back and do the same thing," she said.
Nell said the python was about a metre-and-a-half in length and believes it would have killed the baby koala but not been able to swallow it.
"That was the best feeling in the world … the snake was fine and can find a smaller meal somewhere else."
Nell said she wanted to post the video to create more awareness about the endangered species and the challenges they face.

articles.title_zh: Panda fans flock to Zoo Atlanta for the debut of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang
articles.content_orig:
The six-year-old male and female duo arrived in the US from China under a 10-year loan agreement
Zoo Atlanta’s newest pandas munched bamboo and lounged on Friday during their public debut as smiling visitors lined up to welcome them.
Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, arrived in September from China under a 10-year loan agreement, bringing the cuddly black-and-white bears back to the zoo after a two-year absence.
After spending the past weeks getting acclimated to their habitat, the six-year-old pandas greeted visitors in the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove.

articles.title_orig: Badger rescuer criticised by wildlife welfare charities
articles.title_zh: Badger rescuer criticised by wildlife welfare charities
articles.content_orig:
Three wildlife welfare charities have criticised a Scottish ecologist who is hoping to keep a badger he has nursed back to health.
Graeme Wilson was called out to help the badger, named Harriet, after she was found in a cattle trough 300ft (100m) from her sett.
He believes she was hand-reared prior to this and would not survive in the wild. He applied to NatureScot to keep the animal but they turned him down.
In a strongly-worded statement, the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council, Scottish Badgers and the Badgers Trust said the case raised serious animal welfare concerns.
The BWRC, which works in wildlife casualty welfare in the UK, said it had suspended the membership of Wilson as he had not upheld their principles.
They "firmly oppose" the permanent captivity of any native British wild animal and says they should be humanely euthanised in all but exceptional circumstances.
Wilson, who has a licence to keep unreleasable bats, remains defiant and is convinced that he did the right thing.
He runs GW Ecology, a small independent wildlife rehabilitation service at his home in Denholm in the Scottish Borders.
"I've always taken the view that if it cannot be released, but it can be kept humanely in captivity, then that's what would happen," he said.
"If it can't be kept in captivity under humane conditions, then obviously euthanasia is the route to go."
The joint statement from the wildlife charities said it was a "deeply sad outcome" that Harriet had become so used to humans she could not be released into the wild.
"Wildlife rehabilitation is not about hand-rearing animals, becoming attached to them and then deciding they should spend the rest of their lives in captivity because improper practice has made them accustomed to human contact," they said.
"Her finder clearly had a good heart and good intentions but professional help from a reputable licensed wildlife rescue centre with the appropriate facilities should have been sought [when he found her]," they added.
"At that age, whether she was accustomed to humans or not, she should have been rewilded and grouped with other cubs for release later in the year."
They said the options for Harriet were "extremely limited" and include euthanasia or  being placed in a zoo or sanctuary.
"To suggest that a zoo or sanctuary is an appropriate alternative demonstrates a fundamental lack of understanding of the behavioural, social and welfare needs of badgers," they added.
"The current situation with the finder is not acceptable, appropriate or suitable for a badger."
Wilson is clear that the badger had been hand-reared before he was called to rescue her from the cattle trough.
"She was very thin," he said. "She needed critical care formula and food inside her very quickly. That's what happened.
"Over the next few weeks she put on weight. She was not engaged with at all, which was in line with various rehab recommendations."
When he took her back to her sett, he said she tried to climb a tree and "was freaking out" so he felt he had to take her home.
He said he wanted an educational licence so he could show people why it was important they do not hand-rear badgers.
"I didn't hand rear a badger," he said. "I took in a very, very, very ill, very hungry, dehydrated badger into care that had been hand reared... there is quite a big difference there."
The Badger Trust says that if you find an injured or unwell badger, contact a reputable and experienced wildlife rescue centre, a local badger group, the RSPCA or the Scottish SPCA for support.
A cub seen alone is not necessarily orphaned, so seek advice before intervening. If it is safe to do so, keep your distance, note where you found it and what you observed, and keep people and dogs away.
Do not feed it, move it, take it home or handle it. Let experienced rescuers advise on what to do next.
